name: TensorRT-LLM
notable_features: PyExecutor background loop with a Scheduler, KVCacheManager, ModelEngine and Sampler; requests are fetched, scheduled, KV-allocated, then run
Overlap Scheduler is on by default: it launches GPU work for step n+1 while the CPU processes step n, at the cost of one extra decoding step of pipeline depth
CUDA Graph capture with padding up to the nearest captured batch size, documented as worth up to 22% end-to-end throughput on some models
Full parallelism menu: TP, PP, DP, EP, CP and Wide-EP with an expert-parallel load balancer for MoE
Disaggregated prefill/decode serving and day-0 support cadence for new open-weight models
Also hosts a diffusion VisualGen pipeline for image/video generation
hardware_caveats: CUDA only - there is no ROCm, Metal, Vulkan or CPU path. This is the defining constraint of the engine

Version pinning is severe: the pip wheel is built against a specific PyTorch and CUDA Toolkit (docs show CUDA Toolkit 13.1 and a pinned torch cu130 wheel), and a documented failure mode is pip replacing your CUDA-13-compatible torch with a CUDA 12.8 build, leaving an unusable install until you lock torch with a constraints file
The wheel is not interchangeable with the NGC container's torch; inside an NGC PyTorch container you must use the prebuilt wheel shipped at /app/tensorrt_llm instead of the PyPI one
Slurm clusters need MPI rebuilt with Slurm support or the launcher aborts; this is called out as a general MPI+Slurm issue but it bites in practice

DeepGEMM expert-parallel kernels hard-abort after a 60s barrier budget (DG_JIT_BARRIER_TIMEOUT_SECONDS) and the resulting device-side assert poisons the CUDA context, so the first Python traceback points at an unrelated kernel
MoE scaling features (Wide-EP, EPLB, one-sided all-to-all over NVLink, DWDP) are written against NVLink topologies such as NVL72, so their published wins do not transfer to PCIe-only boxes
best_for: Maximum throughput on a fixed NVIDIA fleet, especially MoE models where expert parallelism and load balancing are the bottleneck
Deployments that can afford a build-time/version-lock step in exchange for hand-tuned kernels, CUDA graphs and the overlap scheduler
Latency-bound single-request serving on datacenter NVIDIA parts
avoid_for: Environments where you cannot control the CUDA and PyTorch versions, or where an unexpected pip resolution would be unrecoverable
Teams that need to support many model architectures without NVIDIA adding support for each
notes: 'paged-kv' and 'in-flight batching' both apply: the KVCacheManager allocates blocks and requests are added to a running batch rather than waiting for it to drain. Format support is recorded conservatively - the engine's own quantization path plus Model Optimizer checkpoints (FP8/FP4) are the well-trodden ones. Whether Marlin kernels are selectable inside TRT-LLM was not confirmed from the pages read, so treat that entry as uncertain.
